messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Plumber
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kiet was a 69-year-old South Eastern Asian man who had lived in the United States for many years, worked most of his life as a plumber, and presented for help only after his wife had become concerned about how often he seemed tense and preoccupied even at home. He described a captivity experience from earlier in life that still sat in his mind as something he could not fully place into words. When he tried to speak about it, he said, the story slipped away from him partway through, leaving him with the sense that he knew exactly what had happened but could not find the language to hold it together. In session he would start with a clear account and then lose the thread, pausing, looking down, and saying that the memories came back more as pictures than as a story. He spoke of them as though they were like a film that played over and over, scenes returning without his permission and with the same frightening force each time.

He explained that during the captivity, being surrounded by men had felt especially dangerous, and that this remained true decades later. Even now, if he found himself alone with a group of men, or with a man he did not know well, his attention tightened immediately and he felt a need to keep track of the nearest door. In his work as a plumber, this had become especially difficult in recent years. He often entered unfamiliar houses or commercial spaces with another tradesman or a male supervisor, and before stepping inside he would automatically scan for a way out, as if he needed to know where to go if something turned bad. He had developed the habit of mentally mapping escape routes before crossing a threshold, telling himself it was simply practical. But the habit was so consistent that it shaped how he moved through jobs, making him slower to settle in and more cautious about accepting work that required him to be confined in smaller spaces with other men.

Kiet also described being alert in places that most people associated with safety. He felt on guard even inside his own home, especially when he heard footsteps, voices, or the abrupt sounds of someone moving quickly nearby. Sudden movements by others put him immediately on guard, and he would tense before he had fully registered what he was seeing. His wife had noticed that he was easier to startle and less able to relax in the evenings, sitting with his back to the wall or watching the front door without seeming aware that he was doing it. He did not describe himself as constantly panicked, but he did speak of a persistent readiness, as if his body never fully accepted that he was safe.

Certain physical sensations and bodily reminders also brought the old fear into sharp focus. Nausea, in particular, was upsetting to him. He said that feeling nauseous could make him think back to the captivity, when his body had felt weak, exposed, and out of his control. Neck pain was another reminder that unsettled him. When his neck tightened after a day of work or after sleeping badly, he became wary and more withdrawn, as though the sensation itself carried a message that danger might be near. On those occasions he noticed strong physical reactions when something reminded him of the stressful experience: his body would react before he had time to think, leaving him shaky, tense, and uncomfortable in a way he found hard to settle.

Over the years he had developed ways of keeping the memories at a distance. He said that he detached himself from them, turning his attention away whenever the images began to surface. He avoided dates or anniversaries connected to the event, not because he wished to mark them but because he did not want to spend those days “back there.” He would make himself busy with work, household repairs, or errands so that he did not have to sit still long enough for the images to gather force. These habits had gradually narrowed the places he felt willing to go and the situations he would enter without preparation. He remained devoted to his wife and continued working, but the effort of staying composed took more energy than he admitted to anyone at first.

What finally brought him to treatment was his growing concern that he could not keep these reactions entirely hidden from the people closest to him. His wife had begun telling him that he seemed distant and keyed up, and he had noticed that the old memories were becoming harder to brush away. He came hoping to speak about the captivity without losing the thread and to understand why his body still reacted so sharply to men, sudden movements, nausea, and neck pain. More than anything, he hoped not to feel so on guard in his own home and not to spend the rest of his life arranging doors, exits, and distances as though danger were always about to reappear.
